questions.q: How do you create a new calculated column in a DataFrame?
options: Assign an expression to a column name that doesn't exist yet, e.g. df["Profit"] = df["Revenue"] - df["Cost"]
Use a special .create_column() function
New columns can only be added by importing a new CSV file
Calculated columns require writing a for loop over every row
questions.explain: Assigning to a new column name creates it automatically, applying the expression row by row without any loop needed.

questions.q: Can a calculated column reference another calculated column you just created?
options: Yes — Profit Margin % can be built directly from the Profit column created in the line before it
No, calculated columns can only reference original, unmodified columns
Only if the two columns are created in the exact same line
This causes an error in Pandas
questions.explain: As long as a column already exists in the DataFrame by the time the next line runs, it can be referenced — including a column created moments earlier in the same script.

questions.q: What does .round(1) do to a calculated column?
options: Rounds each value to one decimal place, making results like 41.666666... display as 41.7
Removes the column entirely
Converts the column to an integer with no decimal places
Rounds to the nearest whole number of rows
questions.explain: round(1) keeps one decimal place — a readability habit that avoids displaying long, hard-to-read repeating decimals.

questions.q: How does creating a Pandas calculated column compare to Power Query's Custom Column or a DAX calculated column?
options: All three compute a new value per row from other columns in that row — just with different syntax and at different points in the pipeline
They are completely unrelated concepts with no overlap
Only DAX can actually perform row-by-row calculations
Power Query custom columns and Pandas calculated columns work in fundamentally opposite ways
questions.explain: The underlying idea is identical across all three tools — a per-row calculation referencing other columns — this lesson is really the same pattern in a third syntax.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what does df["Profit"] = df["Revenue"] - df["Cost"] actually do across the whole DataFrame?
options: Subtracts Cost from Revenue for every row automatically, without needing a manual loop
Subtracts Cost from Revenue for only the first row
Creates a single value representing total profit across all rows combined
Requires a separate .apply() call to work correctly
questions.explain: Pandas applies the subtraction across every row automatically, matching each row's Revenue with that same row's Cost — no explicit iteration required.
